children: By Kelly Cloonan
Uber Technologies and British startup Wayve are rolling out their robotaxi service in London, securing a headstart in a key battleground for autonomous-vehicle players.

Starting Thursday, passengers using Uber's app in the U.K. capital could be matched with a vehicle outfitted with Wayve's autonomous-driving technology. However, the service will come with a human driver behind the wheel to monitor and take over if needed, as the companies work to secure further regulatory approvals for fully driverless operations.

The offering marks the first time AVs will be broadly available in London--an important milestone, given the city is tougher for AVs to navigate than more established robotaxi hubs, Wayve's Chief Executive Alex Kendall said.

Compared with San Francisco, for instance, London has more than 15 times as many cyclists and pedestrians on the road, Kendall said. It also tends to have some tougher traffic intersections, such as roundabouts, than the grid-like streets in more modern cities, he said.
"When you add all that up, it is a pretty complex environment to drive in, but one that our AI is able to do very elegantly," Kendall said in an interview.
Other players, such as Baidu and Alphabet's Waymo, are testing their AVs on London's streets as they race to secure a foothold in the city.
Sarfraz Maredia, who leads Uber's autonomous mobility and delivery business, expects the rollout in London to be key as the company looks to scale up its robotaxi offerings in other major cities.
"To show that this technology can work safely and reliably, you need to be able to demonstrate that in the larger, more complex markets," Maredia said in an interview.
"If you can do that in a place like London, that's a pretty strong proof point that you could do it basically anywhere," he added.

Uber has teamed up with dozens of AV partners across its ride-hailing and delivery services as it contends with investor worries over disruption from robotaxi operators offering their services directly to consumers. The company said it is on track to facilitate AV trips in as many as 15 cities globally by the end of this year.
Through its partnership with Wayve, announced in 2024, Uber plans to eventually put the startup's vehicles on its network in 12 markets around the world, starting with London.

More than 140,000 users in London have already opted in to boost their chances of getting matched with a Wayve vehicle, the companies said. They had piloted the service with some of those users after securing permits to offer supervised robotaxi rides from London's transport authority last month.
Still, a fully driverless offering in the city could remain a ways off.

Kendall said talks with London's transport authority to get the necessary approvals are continuing. He declined to share expectations around the timeline for offering the service without a human supervisor.
"There's good alignment about what is needed from the regulators that we work with, like the ones in the U.K., and clear expectation of what's needed technically," Kendall said.
U.K. regulators said the service's launch cements Wayve as a technology trailblazer in the country.

"This is a major milestone for the future of transport in London, as British innovation brings this technology onto our roads and gives passengers more choice," Secretary of State for Transport Heidi Alexander said.

The launch marks the first time Wayve's technology has been available commercially. The startup, which is headquartered in London, has been testing its artificial-intelligence technology on the city's roads since 2018. Its latest funding--a $1.2 billion Series D round disclosed earlier this year, with participation from Uber--brought its post-money valuation to $8.6 billion.
On Wednesday, Uber said it would lay off about 10% of its staff to trim management layers and streamline divisions, with plans to reinvest the savings in its future.
